\section*{Summary}

Both models train the same spiking network (784--128--10 LIF neurons, $T=25$ rate-coded time steps, MNIST, 50
epochs). The backprop model trains it with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time; ours uses only local
three-factor updates and makes no autograd call during training (checked on every run). Since the first
version of this report, our method changed in three ways: a leaky (non-spiking) read-out with Kolen-Pollack
feedback, homeostasis (firing-rate floor and adaptive thresholds) in place of the diversity term, and a faster
implementation of the same update. Every run now uses batch 256.

Results are reported as two comparisons, because the energy term $E$ that our method pays can also be added to
backprop's loss:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Comparison 1, against standard backprop}: our dense configuration (energy weight $\mu = 0$).
  \item \textbf{Comparison 2, against backprop trained with the same energy term}: our sparse configuration
    ($\mu = 10^{-4}$), at matched sparsity. Backprop's learning rate is tuned for this setting. This comparison
    isolates the learning rule from the objective.
\end{itemize}

Across the four fronts (Table~\ref{tab:overview}): accuracy is tied in both comparisons (paired gaps $-0.03 \pm
0.07$ and $-0.05 \pm 0.10$ points). Training is 28\% faster per step against standard backprop and 42\% faster
against backprop with the energy term, with 23\% and 37\% less GPU energy per step. Against standard backprop we
use 3$\times$ fewer synaptic operations and our credit is far more faithful; against backprop with the energy
term, sparsity is matched, backprop's credit is the more faithful one, and our network is more robust to losing
neurons. Our method uses more peak memory in the training step (+18\% and +6\%), and is behind on Fashion-MNIST
($-0.75$ points against standard backprop) and with three hidden layers ($-1.25$ points).

\section*{Comparison 1: standard backprop vs.\ our method (dense)}

Ours: three-factor rule, leaky read-out, Kolen-Pollack feedback (decay $10^{-3}$), SGD with momentum 0.9 at
learning rate 0.2, energy weight $\mu = 0$, quadratic barrier, firing-rate floor 0.01, adaptive thresholds
(target 5\%). Backprop: Adam, learning rate $10^{-3}$, same network and read-out. Both: learning rate halved after
5 epochs without validation improvement.

{\small
\noindent\textbf{Accuracy (all on the 10,000 test images, from the best-validation checkpoint):}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Test accuracy (\%):} The share of test images classified correctly. The prediction is whichever
    of the 10 read-out neurons accumulated the most membrane potential over the 25 time steps. Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Balanced accuracy (\%):} Accuracy computed separately for each digit, then averaged, so every
    digit counts equally. Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Macro precision (\%):} For each digit, the share of images the model labelled with that digit that
    really were that digit; averaged over the 10 digits. Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Macro recall (\%):} For each digit, the share of images of that digit the model found; averaged
    over the 10 digits. Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Macro F1 (\%):} The harmonic mean of precision and recall per digit, averaged over the 10 digits.
    Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Best validation accuracy (\%):} The highest accuracy on the 5,000-image validation set over all
    epochs. That epoch's checkpoint is the one tested.
  \item \textbf{Final training accuracy (\%):} Accuracy on the training images during the last epoch, averaged
    across its batches. Compared with test accuracy it shows how closely a model fits its training data: 100.0\%
    vs.\ 97.6\% for backprop, 97.9\% vs.\ 97.6\% for ours. Descriptive; there is no better direction.
  \item \textbf{Best epoch:} The epoch where validation accuracy peaked. Our method often peaks earlier and then
    loses some validation accuracy over the remaining epochs (an open problem, see the last section).
\end{itemize}

\noindent\textbf{Calibration (does a model's confidence match how often it is right?):}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{ECE, temperature-scaled (expected calibration error):} Test predictions are grouped into 15 bins
    by confidence. In each bin, the gap between average confidence and actual accuracy is taken, and the gaps are
    averaged, weighted by bin size. Zero means perfectly calibrated. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Brier score, temperature-scaled:} The mean squared error between the predicted probabilities for
    the 10 digits and the true answer. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{NLL (negative log-likelihood), temperature-scaled:} The average of $-\log p(y_{\mathrm{true}})$.
    Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Fitted temperature $\tau$:} Probabilities are $\mathrm{softmax}(\text{read-out evidence}/\tau)$,
    with $\tau$ chosen on the validation set to minimize NLL; the three metrics above use it. Descriptive.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\textbf{Decision timing:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Decision step, mean:} For each test image, the earliest of the 25 steps after which the
    prediction never changes again, averaged over images. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Images with no output evidence (\%):} The share of test images for which no hidden spike reached
    the read-out, so its membrane stayed at zero and the prediction defaults to digit 0. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Autograd calls in training (per seed):} How many times PyTorch's backpropagation engine was
    called during training. Backprop calls it once per batch (214 batches $\times$ 50 epochs = 10,700). Ours must
    be 0; this is the check that our method uses no backprop.
\end{itemize}
}

{\small
\noindent\textbf{Training and inference cost, as measured inside the training runs:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Training time, total and per epoch (s):} Time spent on training batches, excluding validation
    passes and checkpoint saving. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Validation time per epoch (s):} One pass over the 5,000 validation images. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Training GPU energy (kJ):} GPU energy over the whole training loop (including validation), read
    from the GPU's own counter. GPU only. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Peak GPU memory, training / validation / test inference (MiB):} The most GPU memory allocated at
    once in that phase. Lower is better.
  \item \textbf{Test inference latency, throughput and GPU energy:} Classifying the 10,000 test images in batches
    of 256 after warm-up. These single measurements are noisy; Table~\ref{tab:t1-bench} measures cost under
    controlled conditions.
  \item \textbf{Hidden-layer firing rate, test (\%):} The average share of time steps on which a hidden neuron
    spikes. Fewer spikes means less work on hardware that only computes when a neuron fires. Lower is sparser.
    (The read-out is non-spiking, so it has no firing rate.)
\end{itemize}
}

models interleaved with the order rotated each repeat. One training step is a forward pass plus the model's own
update (backprop includes its backward pass). Synaptic operations count, per test image, how many synapses are
activated by spikes: a spike of a neuron with $n$ outgoing synapses counts $n$. ``Network'' counts the spikes of
hidden neurons; ``total'' adds the input layer, which is identical for both models.

{\small
\noindent\textbf{Eligibility-Shapley faithfulness ($k=64$):} The proposal's credit score $\varphi_i = \langle G_i,
\Delta W_i\rangle$, computed during training, ranks the 128 hidden neurons; the table silences half of them. If the
credit is faithful, removing the top-credited neurons hurts most. For our method it now does (51.8\% after removing
the top 64 vs.\ 62.6\% after removing 64 random ones); for backprop it does not (87.9\% vs.\ 80.6\%). In the first
version of this report the score was unfaithful for both. Gini: how concentrated credit is (0 = equal, 1 = one
neuron gets all). Stability: rank correlation of the credit between the last two epochs; both remain low.
}

Accuracy after removing a random 25\% (\%)$^d$ & $\boldsymbol{92.8 \pm 1.0}$ & $81.3 \pm 6.1$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

{\small
\noindent\textbf{Credit quality and robustness:} Removing half the layer (previous table) is too coarse at other
widths, and the faithfulness margin also rewards networks that concentrate their computation in a few neurons.
This table adds two measures:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Faithfulness margin, 25\% removed:} Accuracy after removing 32 random neurons minus after removing
    the 32 top-credited ones. Positive means the credit finds the important neurons. Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Credit vs.\ single-neuron removal (Spearman):} Each neuron is removed on its own and the increase in
    test loss is measured; the score is the rank correlation between that measured effect and the credit. It tests
    the credit directly, whatever the network's structure. Higher is better.
  \item \textbf{Accuracy after removing the top-credited / a random 25\%:} The first is descriptive (it shows how
    much a network depends on its most important neurons); the second measures robustness to losing neurons
    (higher is better).
\end{itemize}
Our credit is more faithful and better aligned with the measured effects (0.81 vs.\ 0.57). Our dense network
concentrates its computation more than backprop's, so it is less robust to losing a random quarter of its
neurons (81.3\% vs.\ 92.8\%).
}

\section*{Comparison 2: backprop with the same energy term vs.\ our method (sparse)}

Both models minimize the task loss plus $\mu E_{\mathrm{met}}$ with $\mu = 10^{-4}$, where $E_{\mathrm{met}}$ is the
proposal's metabolic energy (spike, membrane and weight costs, same coefficients). Backprop computes its gradient
with autograd; ours uses closed-form local signals. Backprop: Adam, learning rate $3\cdot 10^{-4}$, the best of
$\{3\cdot10^{-4}, 10^{-3}, 3\cdot10^{-3}\}$ by validation (97.12\%, 96.81\% and 96.26\% test). Ours: as in
comparison 1, with $\mu = 10^{-4}$ and adaptive thresholds off (with the penalty on, a fixed 5\% threshold target
works against it), using the reverse-time form of the same update (identical gradients, less memory). The metric
definitions are those of comparison 1.

{\small
\noindent\textbf{Reading the explainability results at matched sparsity:} Under the energy penalty, backprop
concentrates its computation: removing its top-credited quarter leaves 49.0\% accuracy, and many of its neurons can
be removed at almost no cost, so any reasonable credit identifies the important ones (25\% margin 0.41, Spearman
0.93). Our sparse network spreads its computation (81.4\% after removing the top quarter), which lowers the margin
(0.10) but makes it more robust to random neuron loss (91.4\% vs.\ 89.5\%). Its credit still tracks the measured
removal effects well (0.84). At $k = 64$, the training-time Eligibility-Shapley score is faithful for ours and not
for backprop.

layer, which then stays dense. In both cases our training step is 33--40\% faster.

\section*{Open problems and caveats}

{\small
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Late-training decline.} Our validation accuracy often peaks early (sometimes by epoch 8--10) and
    then declines by up to 2 points by epoch 50; backprop does not show this. The best checkpoint is reported, so an
    early peak costs test accuracy. Fixing it is the most direct route from a tie to an accuracy advantage.
  \item \textbf{Memory.} Our training step uses more memory than backprop's (eligibility information for every
    time step). The reverse-time form reduces the gap from +18\% to +6\% but is not yet adopted for the dense
    configuration, where all three of its seeds peaked early.
  \item \textbf{Implementation dependence.} Both models share the same Python-loop forward pass, where most of the
    time is kernel-launch overhead. A compiled implementation of either model could change the speed ratio.
  \item \textbf{Scope.} MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, fully connected networks with up to three hidden layers.
\end{itemize}
}
